title: Relations and Functions
tagline: Ordered pairs, Cartesian product, relations as subsets, functions, domain, co-domain, range, and standard real-valued functions.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Mathematics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A relation is a way of linking elements of one set to elements of another. That idea is everywhere in mathematics, but it is not yet specific enough to describe a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. A function is the special kind of relation that does that. In this chapter you meet ordered pairs, the Cartesian product of sets, relations as subsets of a Cartesian product, and then functions with their domain, co-domain and range. The chapter also looks at several standard real-valued functions whose graphs and domain/range behaviour are worth knowing.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Ordered pairs; Cartesian product; relation as a subset; domain, co-domain, range; function as a relation with exactly one output per input; standard real-valued functions and their graphs

learningOutcomes: Form ordered pairs and Cartesian products of sets.
Describe a relation as a subset of a Cartesian product and identify its domain, co-domain and range.
Decide whether a given relation is a function and justify the decision.
Find the domain and range of several standard real-valued functions and interpret their graphs.

blocks.text: An ordered pair is a pair of elements written in a fixed order, so the pair (1, 2) is not the same as (2, 1) unless the two entries happen to be equal. The Cartesian product of two sets A and B is the set of all ordered pairs whose first element comes from A and whose second element comes from B. This product is the playground on which relations and functions are built.

items: An ordered pair is written with a fixed order: order matters.
A x B is the set of ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B.
If A has m elements and B has n elements, then A x B has m x n elements.
A x B and B x A are generally different.

items.text: If A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y}, then A x B = {(1, x), (1, y), (2, x), (2, y)}. B x A is different: it is {(x, 1), (x, 2), (y, 1), (y, 2)}.
items.note: Swapping the sets swaps the order in every pair, so the Cartesian product is not symmetric in general.

blocks.text: A relation from set A to set B is any subset of A x B. That is a very general idea. It allows one element of A to be linked to several elements of B, to none at all, or to exactly one. Because of this generality, not every relation is a function. To reason about a relation, it helps to list its ordered pairs, draw an arrow diagram, or describe it by a condition.

items: A relation from A to B is a subset of A x B.
The domain of a relation is the set of first coordinates that appear.
The co-domain is the set B we are relating into.
The range is the set of second coordinates that actually appear.

items.text: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {a, b}, then R = {(1, a), (2, a), (3, b)} is a relation from A to B. Its domain is A, its co-domain is B, and its range is {a, b}.
items.note: The domain is the set of inputs used, the range is the set of outputs actually reached, and the co-domain is the target set we started with.

blocks.text: A function is a relation in which every element of the domain is paired with exactly one element of the co-domain. This is the key restriction. A relation may send one input to several outputs, but then it is not a function. Functions also have a precise language: the domain is the set of all inputs, the co-domain is the specified target set, and the range is the set of outputs actually attained. The range may be smaller than the co-domain.

items: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain.
Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.
Co-domain and range are not the same thing in general.
The range depends on which outputs actually occur.

items.text: If f : R -> R is defined by f(x) = x^2, the domain is all real numbers and the co-domain is all real numbers, but the range is [0, infinity), because a square is never negative and every non-negative real number is a square of some real input.
items.note: This example is a good test of the co-domain vs range distinction: the function never produces a negative output.

blocks.text: Several functions appear so often that it is worth knowing their names, their graphs and their domain/range behaviour. Among the common ones are the constant function, identity function, polynomial functions, rational functions, modulus function, signum function, exponential function, logarithmic function and greatest-integer function. The graph often makes the behaviour much clearer than words alone.

items: Constant function: same output for every input.
Modulus function: outputs the non-negative size of a number.
Greatest-integer function: gives the greatest integer less than or equal to the input.
Exponential and logarithmic functions have restricted ranges or domains, so their graphs are good to know.

items.text: The modulus function f(x) = |x| maps -3 to 3 and 2 to 2. Its graph is a V shape, and its range is all non-negative reals.
items.note: The modulus removes the sign, so the range cannot include negative numbers.

figures.caption: Figure: Relation versus function
figures.description: An arrow diagram showing a relation that is not a function next to one that is a function, with one input mapped to two outputs in the first case.

keyPoints: An ordered pair keeps its order; (a, b) is not generally the same as (b, a).
A x B is the set of all ordered pairs with first component in A and second in B.
A relation from A to B is a subset of A x B.
A function is a relation that assigns exactly one output to each input.
Co-domain is the target set; range is the set of outputs actually reached.
Standard real-valued functions are worth learning by name, graph and domain/range behaviour.
examFocus: If asked for the range, give the actual outputs, not the co-domain; the two are often not equal.
To show a relation is a function, check that no input has more than one output.

vocabulary.meaning: A pair of elements written in fixed order, so the order matters.
The set of all ordered pairs formed from two sets.
A subset of a Cartesian product linking elements of one set to elements of another.
The set of all inputs in a relation or function.
The target set into which a function is declared to map.
The set of outputs actually taken by a function.

questions.prompt: If A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y}, then A x B has how many elements?
questions.explanation: A has 2 elements and B has 2 elements, so A x B has 2 x 2 = 4 ordered pairs.
questions.commonMistake: Adding the set sizes instead of multiplying them.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a function?
options: Every input has at least one output
Every input has exactly one output
Every output has exactly one input
A function cannot be given by ordered pairs
questions.answer: Every input has exactly one output
questions.explanation: The defining property of a function is that each input has exactly one output.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking a function means every output has exactly one input, which is different.

questions.prompt: Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {a, b}. Consider R = {(1, a), (2, a), (3, b)}. Then the range of R is:
questions.explanation: The range is the set of second coordinates that actually appear: a and b.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the co-domain instead of the range, or listing the domain.

questions.prompt: Is the relation {(2, 1), (2, 4)} from real numbers to real numbers a function? Give a reason.
questions.answer: No, because the input 2 is paired with two different outputs, 1 and 4.
questions.explanation: A function must assign exactly one output to each input, so one input having two outputs rules it out.
questions.commonMistake: Saying it is a function because each entry is an ordered pair.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = |x|, what is the range if the domain is all real numbers?
questions.answer: The range is all non-negative real numbers, [0, infinity).
questions.explanation: The modulus function never produces a negative value, and every non-negative value is achieved.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the whole real line as the range.

questions.prompt: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, B = {a, b, c} and R = {(1, a), (2, a), (2, c), (3, b)}. Find the domain, co-domain and range of R, and state whether R is a function from A to B.
questions.answer: Domain of R = {1, 2, 3}; co-domain = {a, b, c}; range = {a, b, c}. R is not a function from A to B because 2 is paired with two different outputs, a and c, and 4 is not paired with any output.
questions.explanation: The domain comes from the first coordinates, the range from the second coordinates, the co-domain is B, and a function from A to B must assign exactly one output to every element of A.
questions.commonMistake: Calling R a function just because each ordered pair looks fine individually, or forgetting to check both that one input has no two outputs and that every element of A is used.
